Abstract

Simulation games are built from a shared but undocumented vocabulary of rule-systems. This report makes that vocabulary explicit and machine-readable, then asks how mathematical, AI, ML, and LLM results from 2019 to 2026 change it. We decompose 174 simulation games (1968 to 2026, 31 subgenres) into 199 atomic mechanics, analyze each mechanic on its own (definition, levers, failure modes, dynamics, mathematical basis, and six anchored scores), map 45 techniques onto mechanics through 218 typed effect edges, and synthesize 42 design opportunities, each with a validation experiment and a dated, falsifiable prediction. All results are projections of a versioned dataset with provenance for every entity and a validator that keeps the report, wiki, tables, and graph consistent.

Findings.

  1. Simulation games are compositions of six layers: substrate, dynamics, coupling, control, legibility, and pacing. Clustering games by the mechanics they use recovers design families (minds, planned economies, build-and-test, hands-on work, authored decisions, generated worlds) that cut across market subgenres; 14 of 16 clusters mix subgenres.
  2. The vocabulary was set early. 68 percent of mechanics appear in a catalog game released by 2000. 34 mechanics first appear in 2010 or later, and 27.5 percent of possible mechanic pairs have ever co-occurred.
  3. Depth costs legibility. On rubric scores from a single model rater, legibility falls as emergence potential rises (ρ = -0.42) and as compute cost rises (ρ = -0.35); emergence rises with tuning difficulty (ρ = 0.61).
  4. AI techniques target what games show and say, not what they are built from. Exposure concentrates in narrative, control, agent, and physics mechanics. 99 mechanics, carrying 51 percent of all mechanic uses in the catalog, are affected by no technique in the set. Explanation is the rarest effect a technique has on a mechanic (5 of 218 edges).
  5. What shipped mostly stays at the edge of simulation state. Neural rendering, asset and motion generation, and language characters for dialogue and companionship have shipped. The shipped techniques that write into game state are narrow: cached model outputs as crafting rules, language-model characters in a few titles, and learned or search-based opponents. Frame-generating world models and learned physics remain prototypes or research. Of the 34 techniques that can run during play, 10 break reproducibility outright.
  6. The best near-term opportunities keep the simulation symbolic and let learned models read, explain, decorate, and propose through validated, logged interfaces. The highest-priority opportunity is Why-query over the simulation log.

The dataset, schemas, contract, and every projection are open for extension; the procedure for contributors, human or agent, is in AGENTS.md.

1. Introduction

A simulation game is a game whose state changes by rules the player did not author and does not fully control. The player builds a road and the traffic is the city's reply; the player sets a tax and the citizens decide whether to stay. Everything distinctive about the form follows from that gap between intent and outcome: the pleasure of watching a system respond, the frustration of not understanding why it did, and the stories players tell about runs no designer scripted.

The genre is old and large. Its lineage runs from text programs on mainframes (a grain-and-population ledger in Hamurabi, a wagon party's rations in The Oregon Trail) through SimCity and The Sims to Dwarf Fortress, Factorio, and EVE Online. Its methods are less visible than its titles. Designers share a working vocabulary (needs meters, production chains, storytellers, overlays) but no common, inspectable map of which rule-systems exist, which games combine them, how each one fails, and which are near their ceilings.

That map matters now because the ceilings are moving. For forty years the depth of a simulation game was bounded by a few constraints: how much compute a consumer machine could spend per tick, how much content a studio could author, how much hidden state a player could understand, how tightly a multiplayer game had to stay deterministic, and how believable a rule-driven agent could be. Results from 2019 to 2026 in learned world models, language-model agents, learned physics, accelerated simulation, automated design, and on-device inference press on each of those constraints, unevenly and with new costs.

This report does four things:

  1. Catalogs 174 simulation games across 31 subgenres, from 1968 to 2026, and decomposes each into the mechanics it uses (1952 typed game-to-mechanic edges, each marked core or supporting, with implementation notes for core mechanics).
  2. Analyzes 199 mechanics one at a time: rule-level definition, player experience, design levers, failure modes, dynamics, mathematical basis, and six anchored scores (legibility, emergence potential, authoring cost, compute cost, tuning difficulty, AI leverage).
  3. Maps 45 mathematical, AI, ML, and LLM techniques onto those mechanics through 218 typed affects edges that say how each technique changes each mechanic (replaces its substrate, deepens it, enables a new form, cuts its authoring cost, explains it, tunes it, or accelerates it).
  4. Synthesizes 42 design opportunities, each with a validation experiment a small team could run and a falsifiable prediction with a resolve-by date.

Every number in this document is rendered from the dataset at build time; the dataset hash on the title page identifies the exact version. The report, the wiki, the tables, and the graph are projections of the same YAML files, so a correction to one entity updates all of them.

2. Method

2.1 Unit of analysis: the mechanic

A mechanic here is a rule-system that passes four admission tests (CONTRACT.md, I12):

  • Nameable. Designers would recognize it in games other than the one being examined.
  • Atomic. It owns one kind of state and one update rule. If it splits into two parts that each appear without the other in shipped games, it is two mechanics.
  • Tunable. It has at least two levers.
  • Removable. A game could drop it and keep running.

The tests exclude two common confusions. Dynamics such as "cascading failure" or "death spiral" are outcomes of coupled mechanics, so they appear in mechanics' dynamics fields rather than as entities. Genre-level patterns such as "colony management" are combinations, so they appear as game decompositions or opportunities. The result sits between the MDA framework's mechanics layer and a designer's pattern language: concrete enough to implement, general enough to recur.

Each mechanic belongs to one of 21 families, assigned by the state it owns rather than the genre it appears in: Weather is environment, Labor market is economy, Agent inspection is information.

2.2 Corpus

The game catalog was built to cover every subgenre in the vocabulary, every lineage-defining title from the 1960s onward, recent releases through 2026, research demonstrations that run as interactive simulations (such as Generative Agents (Smallville) and Project Sid), and works included for a single mechanic (marked boundary_case; 21 such works). The catalog is a purposive sample, not a census: prevalence figures describe this corpus, and the earliest-appearance year of a mechanic is a lower bound on its true origin.

2.3 Schema and scoring

Every categorical field draws from a closed vocabulary (vocab/), and every ordinal field names an anchored rubric (vocab/rubrics.yaml). Scorers match the anchor text and take the lower anchor when between two. This trades resolution for consistency across contributors: a 3 in legibility means "understood after deliberate attention and the game's info tools" whoever assigned it. Every score in this version was assigned by one model rater (claude-opus-5-5) matching the anchor text; scores are judgments, not measurements, and the rubric for each is reproduced in the wiki.

Relations are typed edges with one owner each (vocab/edge_types.yaml). Inverses (which games use a mechanic, which techniques affect it) and all aggregates (prevalence, earliest appearance, clusters, technique exposure, opportunity priority) are computed by the build and never stored, so they cannot drift from the edges they summarize.

2.4 Evidence

Each entity carries an epistemic status. asserted means written from domain knowledge without a citation; sourced means at least one cited source supports its factual fields; verified requires a second, independent run. Techniques must always cite. At this version, 388 entities are sourced or verified and 71 remain asserted; the asserted ones form a public verification queue (dist/analysis/verification-queue.csv).

2.5 Production

The dataset was produced by parallel research runs, each recorded in log/runs/ with its operator, model, method, and the proposals it could not act on. Parallel runs partitioned work by file, not by topic: taxonomy runs analyzed mechanics; catalog runs verified release facts against public sources and decomposed games; technique runs searched the 2019 to 2026 literature and developer announcements. Merge-time runs then edited entities across partitions: the synthesis run added symmetric synergy and tension edges in one pass, and a review run added mechanic tags to games after an independent review found widely shared mechanics (pause controls, placement, tech trees) under-tagged, recoded several decompositions, and tightened every prediction. Each cross-partition edit is attributed in the entity's provenance.reviewed list. A validator enforcing the rules in CONTRACT.md §5 gated every merge. The same procedure (AGENTS.md) is what a new contributor, human or agent, follows.

2.6 Limitations

  • Sampling. Commercial, English-language, PC-centric titles are over-represented; mobile management games and non-Western simulation traditions are under-represented.
  • Scoring. Rubric scores are single-rater judgments by one model (claude-opus-5-5), not independent expert ratings. Correlations among scores (§5.6) and between a score and the technique graph (§8.4) partly reflect that rater's internal consistency. The verified status and the review field exist so a second rater, human or model, can confirm or contest them.
  • Decomposition depth. A game's mechanic list records what is present and meaningful, not a complete specification. Absence of an edge is weak evidence of absence.
  • Recency. Technique maturity and horizon are judged as of the run date and age quickly; each technique records the sources the judgment rests on.

3. The catalog

The corpus spans 1968 to 2026. Its oldest entries are text programs written for teaching (Hamurabi, The Oregon Trail, Lemonade Stand) and a zero-player automaton (Conway's Game of Life); its newest are releases from 2024 to 2026 and research demonstrations whose agents are language models.

4. A grammar of simulation games

4.1 Six layers

Decomposing the catalog suggests that every simulation game is assembled from six layers. A mechanic usually lives in one layer, and a game's character comes from which layers it invests in.

  1. Substrate: what exists. State is held as aggregate stocks (a treasury, a population count), individual agents (a colonist with needs), fields on a grid (pollution, temperature, land value), networks (roads, pipes, social ties), or continuous bodies (a wing, a chassis). The substrate fixes the cost curve: aggregates are cheap and faceless, agents are expensive and legible, fields scale with map area, continuous physics scales with contacts and timestep. The substrate field on every mechanic records this (
Substratemechanics
Rule system107
Agent-based70
Aggregate stocks69
Cellular grid38
Stochastic events33
Network / graph31

Player-authored logic9
UI layer9
Learned model4

). 2. Dynamics: how it changes. Update rules form feedback loops. Most simulation games pair a reinforcing growth loop (more citizens, more taxes, more buildings) with balancing loops that resist it (congestion, pollution, unrest, raids). Difficulty is the relative strength of those loops; a death spiral is a reinforcing loop running in reverse. The feedback field records the dominant polarity per mechanic. 3. Coupling: how subsystems touch. Depth comes less from the number of systems than from how many share state. Systems couple through shared stocks (power, money, labor), shared space (a factory lowers neighboring land value), and shared agents (the same colonist hauls, eats, and grieves). Dwarf Fortress is deep because nearly everything touches nearly everything else; a game with many isolated systems feels like many small games. 4. Control: how intent enters. The player acts directly (an avatar, a unit), places and zones, sets parameters, issues orders that agents pick up, writes programs, or speaks. Each step away from direct control widens the control gap, the designed distance between what the player wants and what happens. Too narrow and the game is a toy; too wide and the player is a spectator.

  1. Legibility: how state leaves. Overlays, inspectors, tooltips, advisors, alerts, graphs, chronicles, and forecasts expose hidden state. This layer is what lets deep simulations ship: RimWorld itemizes every mood modifier, and Paradox games nest tooltips until each number decomposes into causes. Legibility mechanics own no simulation state of their own; they are the interface between coupling and comprehension.
  2. Pacing and stakes: when the player looks and what can be lost. Time models (pause, speed, turns, wall clock), failure models (soft setbacks, permadeath, cascading collapse), and narrative directors decide when attention is demanded and what a mistake costs.

A compact description of a simulation game is its investment profile across these layers. City builders invest in substrate (fields and networks) and legibility (overlays); colony sims in agents, coupling, and pacing (storytellers); vehicle sims in continuous substrate and direct control; programming games in control alone, with nearly no hidden state. The clustering in §5 recovers these profiles from the data without being told the subgenres.

4.2 The families, one at a time

Each family below is described by the state it owns, its canonical mechanics, how it characteristically fails, and what it couples to. Tables list every mechanic in the family with how many catalog games use it and its rubric scores; each mechanic's full analysis (definition, levers, failure modes, dynamics, open questions) is on its wiki page.

Resources and production

Owns stocks of goods and the recipes that transform them. Production chains is the backbone of city builders, factory games, and colony sims alike; Storage and buffers, Spoilage, and Byproducts and waste decide whether a chain is a puzzle or a ledger. The characteristic failure is the spreadsheet: chains whose only decision is ratio arithmetic. The best implementations make chains spatial (Conveyor transport) or social (who does the work, and in what mood).

Logistics and networks

Owns movement across space or graphs: roads, belts, pipes, rails, transit lines, service reach. These mechanics turn production into geography, and they are where compute and legibility first bind: Traffic congestion is the most visible place a city builder can be wrong, and Walker service delivery made service coverage legible by putting it on walking bodies. Networks couple to almost everything, so their bugs (pathfinding loops, gridlock) spread to every system they feed.

Economy and finance

Owns money, prices, and valuation. Most games use only Treasury and budget and Taxation as a scorekeeping layer; fewer simulate markets with Supply-demand pricing, competitors (Rival firms), or player-made prices (Player-driven markets). The characteristic failure is the dominant strategy: a price or loan loophole that converts the economy into an exploit, which is why economies are the first target for automated balancing (§9).

Agents and behavior

Owns individual minds: needs, utilities, moods, memories, skills, schedules. Needs decay plus Utility action selection is the standard architecture since The Sims; Smart objects moved behavior knowledge into the world so new objects bring new behaviors. Its variety is paid for in animations, thoughts, and dialogue, which is why it is among the families most exposed to language-model techniques (§8).

Social relations

Owns ties between agents: relationship values, opinion modifiers, reputation, factions, gossip, romance, and conversation. Rule-based social systems are cheap but read as formulaic; Social exchanges in Prom Week and Versu showed richer social logic is possible at high authoring cost, and Natural-language interaction opened conversation as an input. The characteristic failure is the visible formula: players learn that one compliment always adds a fixed amount.

Population and lineage

Owns birth, death, migration, inheritance, and structure. Immigration by attractiveness is the city builder's growth engine; Population strata turns growth into progression; Trait inheritance and Dynasty succession stretch play across generations. These mechanics define the time horizon of a game more than its time model does.

Governance and policy

Owns rules about rules: policies, laws, elections, interest groups, satisfaction, unrest. Policy menus (Policy toggles) are universal; Policy influence network in Democracy 4 made the causal web itself the interface; Player legislation in Eco and A Tale in the Desert let players write rules for each other. The failure is the menu: a fixed list of authored options that no player can extend.

Physics and materials

Owns continuous dynamics: rigid bodies, vehicles, flight, orbits, fluids, heat, deformation, destruction, material interactions. These are, on average, the most compute-bound mechanics in the taxonomy, and their legibility depends on how closely they match the physical intuitions players bring. The failure is the uncanny edge: a physics model accurate enough to invite intuition but wrong in the cases players probe.

Environment and ecology

Owns the world's own processes: weather, seasons, food webs, habitats, pollution, fire, contagion, water, climate. Environmental mechanics are where simulation games most often lean on real science (Contagion follows compartment models; Food web follows predator-prey dynamics) and where calibrated learned models can substitute for hand-tuned approximations.

Time and pacing

Owns the clock. Pause and speed control is near-universal in real-time management games; Real-time clock ties play to the calendar; Daily action budget makes days a scarce resource; Crisis countdown turns the future into a deadline. Control and automation

Owns the channel from intent to action: avatars, unit commands, designations, programming, circuits, blueprints, delegation, god powers, and embodied skill. The history of the family is a steady move away from direct control toward specification: from clicking each unit to drawing zones, from wiring logic to writing code, and now toward stating intent in language.

5. The structure of the design space

5.1 What games are made of

The average catalog game uses 11.2 mechanics (median 11). The most widely used is Pause and speed control, present in 47 percent of games. The head of the distribution is interface and structure more than simulation: time controls, placement, progression structures (tech trees, scenarios), then production, skills, avatars, and modding. 5.2 How the vocabulary grew

68 percent of mechanics appear in at least one catalog game released by 2000, and 59 percent first appear in the 1980s or 1990s (1990s the largest decade). The early vocabulary came from a short list of titles: SimCity (zoning, land value, overlays, disasters), Populous (terraforming as a god power), Railroad Tycoon and Transport Tycoon (route scheduling and competitors), Theme Park and Theme Hospital (crowds with preferences, queues, diagnosis), Creatures (learning creatures and genetics), and The Sims (smart objects).

Games clustered by weighted Jaccard similarity of mechanic sets (average linkage, k=16, core weight 2.0, inverse-prevalence weighting so ubiquitous mechanics do not dominate). Signature mechanics maximize within-cluster share x log-lift. Members are ordered by centrality (mean distance to the rest of the cluster), so the first members are the most typical.

The clusters read as design families:

  • Minds. Life sims, colony sims, and agent-driven management share the largest cluster, built on utility action selection, personality, and needs: The Sims, RimWorld, Dwarf Fortress, Two Point Hospital. Virtual pets and trainable creatures form a separate cluster on care and learning: Creatures, Tamagotchi, Black & White.
  • Planned economies. City builders split into two lineages: production chains and placement (Anno 1800, Factorio, Manor Lords) and the SimCity line of zoning, land value, and traffic (SimCity, Cities: Skylines). Grand strategy and political city builders cluster on policy and unrest: Europa Universalis IV, Crusader Kings III, Tropico 6, Frostpunk.
  • Build and test. Physics sandboxes and construction games cluster on rigid bodies and signal circuits: Besiege, Teardown, Poly Bridge. Programming puzzles share a cluster with persistent programmable worlds, since both are about systems the player writes and leaves running: SpaceChem, Screeps, EVE Online.
  • Hands-on work. Job sims form their own cluster on surface tools and contracts, apart from the physics sandboxes: PowerWash Simulator, Car Mechanic Simulator 2021, PC Building Simulator. Vehicle and flight sims cluster on embodied skill and weather: iRacing, X-Plane, DCS World.
  • Authored decisions. Inspection and dilemma games cluster on event chains and dilemma cards across subgenres: Papers, Please, Reigns, Suzerain, This War of Mine.
  • Turn reports. The 1970s text sims (Hamurabi, The Oregon Trail, Lemonade Stand) form a cluster on turn structure and random events.
  • Generated worlds. The AI-native titles cluster on generated content and natural-language interaction, apart from the life sims they resemble on the surface: AI Dungeon, Infinite Craft, Suck Up!.

These families match the layer profiles in §4.1: minds invest in agents and social coupling; planned economies in stocks, networks, and legibility; build-and-test games in control and continuous substrate; hands-on work and vehicle sims in direct control and physics.

Section 9 develops several of these as opportunities.

5.6 The legibility frontier

Across all mechanics, legibility and emergence potential are negatively correlated (Spearman ρ = -0.42, p <0.001), and emergence potential is strongly correlated with tuning difficulty (ρ = 0.61, p <0.001). Mechanics that generate unscripted variety are harder to understand and harder to balance. Legibility also falls as compute cost rises (ρ = -0.35, p <0.001): expensive simulation tends to be hidden simulation.

Two caveats bound these numbers. First, every rubric score was assigned by one model rater (claude-opus-5-5) against written anchors, so the correlations describe that rater's reading of design knowledge, not independent expert agreement or player measurement. Second, mechanics in the legibility and time-and-pacing families sit at the bottom of the emergence scale by construction (69 percent score 1), since an overlay or a pause button generates nothing on its own; excluding them leaves the legibility-emergence correlation at ρ = -0.35, weaker but the same sign.

6. Five ceilings

Simulation design has been shaped less by imagination than by five constraints. Each one explains a family of conventions, and each one is the target of a different group of techniques in §7.

6.1 Compute per tick

A consumer machine must advance the whole simulation many times per second while rendering it. The constraint explains why city builders simulate aggregate populations with a sample of visible agents, why per-particle material simulation (Falling-sand materials, Fluid and gas simulation) appears in 2D or small arenas, why late-game slowdown is a genre-wide complaint, and why Agent pathfinding and Traffic congestion are the usual bottlenecks. Mechanics scored 4 or 5 on compute cost are the ones whose scale is capped by hardware rather than design.

Relaxed by: GPU-parallel and accelerated simulation, learned surrogates for physics and weather, mean-field approximations for large populations, and inference-efficient models for agent decisions.

6.2 Authoring cost

Every unit of variety in some mechanics must be made by hand: an animation for each interaction, a line of dialogue for each social exchange, an event for each situation, an asset for each catalog entry. Mechanics with high authoring cost are capped by budgets, and players exhaust them; this is why event decks repeat, why villagers recycle requests, and why social systems in rule-based games read as formulaic. Across mechanics, authoring cost and judged AI leverage have a Spearman correlation of 0.34 (p <0.001): the mechanics most limited by content budgets are, in the rater's judgment, the ones most open to generative techniques. Both scores come from the same model rater (§2.6), so the correlation shows a consistent reading rather than independent confirmation.

Relaxed by: constrained language generation for events and dialogue, text-to-3D and neural rendering for assets, learned motion for animation, and procedural generation with learned priors.

6.3 Legibility

Players must form a working model of why the simulation did what it did, or they experience the depth as randomness. The rubric scores show the tension (§5.6): the mechanics that generate the most unscripted variety are the hardest to understand.

Designers have answered with a whole family of mechanics that own no simulation state (Data overlays, Causal breakdown tooltips, Agent inspection, History chronicle). Each costs design effort and screen space, and each coupled system a game adds needs one.

Relaxed by: language models that read state and event logs and explain causes, forecasting by simulating futures, and learned surrogates that make expensive hidden fields cheap to visualize.

6.4 Determinism

Replays, lockstep multiplayer, bug reproduction, competitive leaderboards, and save integrity require that the same inputs produce the same state. Factorio's multiplayer depends on it. Determinism has kept stochastic or learned components out of authoritative game state. Of the 34 techniques here that can run during play, 10 break reproducibility outright, 16 can be made reproducible by seeding, caching, or logging their outputs, and 8 leave it intact (see determinism_impact).

Relaxed by: recording model outputs as events so replays read the log rather than re-call the model, splitting authoritative symbolic state from non-authoritative generated presentation, and constrained decoding that maps open-ended outputs into typed, validated state changes.

6.5 Believability of agents

Rule-driven agents are legible and cheap but shallow: their utilities are visible formulas and their speech is canned. The constraint shapes the genre's preference for many shallow agents (Crowd preferences) or few agents with thick systemic state (Memories and thoughts, Injury body model) over agents with rich minds.

Relaxed by: language-model agents with memory and reflection, models trained to predict human choices, and small local models that make per-agent language affordable.

6.6 What the ceilings imply

The five constraints do not move together. Authoring cost is being relaxed fastest, with asset, motion, and language techniques already shipped; compute is being relaxed mostly in rendering, not in simulation. Agent believability is being relaxed at a new cost in determinism and legibility. Legibility shows the widest gap between available technique and use (§8.1): explanation over structured state needs retrieval, constrained generation, and summarization, all of which exist.

Of 45 techniques, 1 is shipped as a genre norm, 12 are shipped in at least one commercial game, 10 exist as public prototypes, and 22 are research only. The shipped ones cluster in three places: rendering and assets (Neural rendering in the graphics pipeline, ML reconstruction of the planet from aerial imagery, Text- and image-to-3D asset generation, Learned kinematic motion synthesis), language characters (Generative agents (memory stream, reflection, planning), On-device small language models for characters, Realtime speech-to-speech and expressive TTS for characters, LLM game master and narrative director, LLM-adjudicated state transitions (LLM as game mechanic)), and older search and learning methods (Monte Carlo tree search for game AI, Wave Function Collapse and constraint-based tile generation, Deep reinforcement learning policies for NPC opponents and navigation, Agent-based automated playtesting and balancing). The shipped techniques that write into authoritative state are narrow: LLM-adjudicated state transitions (LLM as game mechanic) stores cached model outputs as Infinite Craft's combination rules, language agents choose actions for characters in inZOI and a few AI-native titles, and search and learned policies drive opponents such as Gran Turismo Sophy in Gran Turismo 7. No learned replacement for physics, fields, or the world itself is deployed in a catalog game.

7.2 Adoption and reception

Generative AI has moved from novelty to a measurable share of releases. Disclosures on Steam rose from about a thousand games in April 2024 [1] to 7,818 titles by July 2025, about 7 percent of the store, with just under a fifth of 2025 releases disclosing [2]; and an estimate in November 2025 put games with disclosures at roughly 8 percent of the store with about 660 million dollars in combined gross [3]. Most disclosures concern pre-generated visual assets rather than runtime systems. Valve's survey distinguishes pre-generated from live-generated content and requires the latter to describe its guardrails [4].

Developer sentiment moved the other way. In GDC's surveys, 36 percent of respondents reported using generative AI themselves in both 2025 and 2026, while the share who believe it harms the industry rose to 52 percent from 30 percent [5, 6]. Player reception has been mixed in visible cases: inZOI sold strongly at launch and drew negative reviews after announcing generative features [7]; ARC Raiders was criticized for synthetic voice lines, some of which were later re-recorded by actors [8].

Runtime language characters did ship. On-device small language models power simulated people in inZOI's Smart Zoi and companions in NARAKA's teammate and the PUBG Ally limited beta of June 2026 [9, 10]; Where Winds Meet discloses live NPC text and voice chat [11]. Audio prices for one leading realtime speech API fell from 100 and 200 dollars per million input and output tokens at launch in October 2024 to 32 and 64 dollars in August 2025, about 68 percent [12, 13], and specialized text-to-speech vendors price in cents per minute [14]. Cost limits frame-generating world models: the consumer Genie product grants sixty seconds of play per world, which DeepMind attributed to reaching more users on limited compute [15].

Among rendering techniques, neural upscaling and frame generation are the one area where learned models are a norm, with hundreds of supported titles [16]. They never touch simulation state, which is why they could spread.

7.3 Seven clusters

Frame-generating world models. Diffusion and autoregressive neural game engines, Genie foundation world models, Muse World and Human Action Model (WHAM), and Open real-time interactive video world models learn to predict the next frame from recent frames and player input, so the model is the engine. They produce convincing short interactions and fail at what simulation games need most: exact persistent state, long memory, and inspectable causes. Their realistic near-term role is ideation, previsualization, and non-authoritative views (§9).

3D, rendering, and assets. 3D Gaussian Splatting, Prompt-to-persistent 3D world generation, Text- and image-to-3D asset generation, Neural rendering in the graphics pipeline, Real-time generative restyling of game video, and ML reconstruction of the planet from aerial imagery cut the authoring cost of what the simulation is drawn with, leaving rules untouched. They are the most mature group. Most preserve determinism; Text- and image-to-3D asset generation and Real-time generative restyling of game video are mitigable, since a generated asset or frame must be stored to be reproduced. Their main risks are provenance and reception.

Motion. Learned kinematic motion synthesis has shipped in sports and life games; Learned physics-based character control remains research. Both matter to simulation games because canned animation is how most agents' internal states are (poorly) displayed.

Language agents and dialogue. Generative agents (memory stream, reflection, planning), Many-agent LLM societies, LLM models of individual human choice, On-device small language models for characters, Grammar-constrained decoding for valid game actions, Realtime speech-to-speech and expressive TTS for characters, LLM game master and narrative director, LLM explanation of simulation state, and LLM-adjudicated state transitions (LLM as game mechanic) change who decides what agents do and say, who narrates, and who explains. They relax the authoring and believability ceilings at a cost in consistency. Their determinism cost varies: Generative agents (memory stream, reflection, planning), Many-agent LLM societies, LLM game master and narrative director, and Realtime speech-to-speech and expressive TTS for characters break reproducibility; On-device small language models for characters and LLM-adjudicated state transitions (LLM as game mechanic) are mitigable because a local model can be seeded and a cached rule is replayed rather than regenerated.

Planning and game theory. Monte Carlo tree search for game AI, Self-play planning with learned models (AlphaZero, MuZero, Dreamer), Regret minimization and search for imperfect-information games, Language models grounded in strategic planning for negotiation games, Deep reinforcement learning policies for NPC opponents and navigation, and Mean field games and mean-field learning produce strong opponents and equilibrium-consistent populations. Their game deployments are few because strength is rarely the design goal; believable and tunable opponents are.

Design automation. Wave Function Collapse and constraint-based tile generation, Quality-diversity search (MAP-Elites) for content and balance, Learned level and map generation (PCGRL, MarioGPT, LLM generators), Automated generation of game rules and mechanics, Agent-based automated playtesting and balancing, Open-ended co-generation of environments and agents, LLM-written skill libraries (Voyager), Generalist instructable game agents (SIMA), and LLM-guided evolutionary program search mostly work on the developer's side: generating content and rules, finding exploits, and estimating difficulty. Used offline they preserve determinism. Some also run during play (Wave Function Collapse and constraint-based tile generation in Townscaper, agents that play alongside the player). Deterministic algorithms such as wave-function collapse stay reproducible there; learned generators and agents need seeds or logs.

Simulation science. Massively parallel GPU simulation, Differentiable simulation, Graph network simulators and neural operators, Subspace neural physics and learned deformers, Machine-learned weather forecasting, Neural cellular automata, Continuous cellular automata and foundation-model search for artificial life, and Simulation-based inference for calibrating simulators come from robotics, physics, climate, and artificial life. They relax the compute ceiling and make calibration possible, and they are the least connected to game development today: an operational ML weather model runs at about a thousandth of the energy of the physics model it complements [17], yet none of these techniques is confirmed at runtime in a catalog game.

8. Where the techniques land

8.1 How techniques change mechanics

Each affects edge records one of seven effects. Across 218 edges the most common effect is deepens (74 edges): the technique makes an existing mechanic richer, larger, or more varied without changing its role. Explanation is the rarest effect (5 edges).

The imbalance shows where research effort points. Generating content and replacing substrates (rule-based behavior with language models, numerical physics with learned dynamics) attract most work; explaining a simulation to the person playing it attracts little, although the techniques it needs (retrieval over structured logs, constrained generation, summarization) exist.

Exposure concentrates in four families: narrative and generation, agents and behavior, control and automation, and physics and materials: the layers where content is expensive to author or where behavior is expensive to compute. Per mechanic, Narrative & generation still leads, so the concentration is not an artifact of family size. Exposure is low across the economic and logistic core of the genre (resources, logistics, economy, population) and lowest of all in operation and procedure. 99 mechanics are affected by no technique in the set, and they account for 51 percent of all game-to-mechanic uses in the catalog. Of the ten most widely used mechanics, 6 have no technique attached.

Current AI research mostly targets what a simulation game shows and says, not the rule-systems most simulation games are built from. That is partly sensible (production chains and budgets are cheap and legible already) and partly a gap: the economic core is where balance work, legibility problems, and authoring of recipes and scenarios consume design time.

Modding interfaces, blueprints, romance and family systems, creature care, diagnosis, product design, history generation, and rule-checking inspection are each judged ready for substantial change, and none has a technique pointed at it in this dataset. Some are covered implicitly by general techniques (code generation for modding, language models for romance dialogue), but none has a cited, game-specific result.

8.5 Authoritative state versus presentation

The techniques divide by whether they touch authoritative simulation state. Those that change only presentation have shipped (neural upscaling and frame generation, asset generation, motion synthesis) or reached prototypes (restyling); they preserve determinism or can be made reproducible by storing what they generate. Those that would replace physics, fields, or the world with learned prediction remain prototypes or research in games. The shipped exceptions that reach state are narrow and controlled: cached model outputs as rules (LLM-adjudicated state transitions (LLM as game mechanic)), language-model characters that choose actions in inZOI (Generative agents (memory stream, reflection, planning), On-device small language models for characters), and opponents (Deep reinforcement learning policies for NPC opponents and navigation, Monte Carlo tree search for game AI). Of these, only the language characters break reproducibility outright. The pattern suggests a design principle that recurs through §9: keep the simulation symbolic, typed, and logged, and let learned models read it, explain it, decorate it, and propose changes to it through validated interfaces.

9.2 Five design principles

The opportunities share a small set of principles, each a response to the ceilings in §6 and the evidence in §8.

  1. Keep the simulation symbolic; let models read, explain, decorate, and propose. Authoritative state stays typed and deterministic. Learned models sit around it as renderers, narrators, explainers, and proposal generators whose outputs pass through validators (Symbolic simulation, neural rendering, Content-elastic event systems, Natural-language legislation).
  2. Spend inference on salience. Most ticks need no model. Calls at moments that matter, cached and logged, buy believability at bounded cost (Salience-gated language agents, Drama-aware storyteller, Local-first AI simulation games).
  3. Explain before you generate. Comprehension limits how much coupling players can use (§6.3), and technique research rarely targets it (§8.1). Explanation over logs and sensitivity analysis needs only techniques that already exist (Why-query over the simulation log, Bottleneck explainer for production networks, Branch preview of policy futures, Illustrated chronicles).
  4. Generate offline, verify with agents. Content, recipes, scenarios, mods, and balance can be generated at design time and checked by automated play before any player sees them (Parallel autobalancing of economies, Generated recipe graphs, Quality-diversity scenario libraries, Mechanic modding by description).
  5. Log every model call as an event. Recording outputs restores replay, multiplayer sync, bug reproduction, and auditability, and the same log powers explanation, forecasting, and chronicles (Event-sourced simulation runtime).

9.3 By the ceiling they relax

Legibility. Why-query over the simulation log answers why-questions from the event log; Bottleneck explainer for production networks points at the binding constraint in production networks, a widely used mechanic with no technique attached; Branch preview of policy futures shows distributions of futures before a decision; Explained delegation to AI managers makes delegated subsystems accountable; Simulator instructor coaching narrates mistakes in operation sims.

Authoring cost. Content-elastic event systems removes the ceiling on event decks; Generated inspection shifts gives rule-checking games endless fair cases; Generative decoration catalogs and Learned build assist for cities widen creative modes; Generated recipe graphs and Quality-diversity scenario libraries cut the cost of progression content; Mechanic modding by description hands extension to players.

Agent believability. Salience-gated language agents gives colony and life sims specific minds at bounded cost; Drama-aware storyteller picks events for characters' arcs; Negotiating faction AI lets rivals bargain and remember; Human-calibrated customers grounds crowds in models of real choice; Trainable creatures revival returns to learned creatures with modern learning; Learned motion for simulated crowds shows internal state in movement.

Compute. Learned material surrogates at world scale extends particle-level materials to whole worlds; Mean-field crowds and traffic lets cities hold equilibrium-consistent populations; Learned regional weather brings realistic weather at low runtime cost.

Determinism and infrastructure. Event-sourced simulation runtime and Local-first AI simulation games make AI components operable in long-lived, offline, moddable games; Symbolic simulation, neural rendering separates what must be exact from what may be generated.

New forms. Language-agent society terrarium makes watching a language-agent society the game; Open-ended evolution sandbox builds evolution games on continuous artificial life; Specification programming games turns programming puzzles into specification and testing; Intent-level orders and Teachable sim companion move control from clicks to intent and demonstration; Agent ambassadors between player worlds links single-player worlds through negotiating envoys; Generated dream and replay views gives world models a role where drift is a feature; Factories with a living workforce, Placement that tells stories, and Research by named scientists fill white space between common mechanics.

Beyond entertainment. Simulation games as agent benchmarks offers simulation games as long-horizon evaluation environments for AI agents; Participatory planning sandboxes and Calibrated serious simulations carry calibrated models into planning and education; Automated mechanic discovery uses this taxonomy as a search space for new mechanics.

9.4 Where to start, by kind of builder

  • A small studio should look first at opportunities with feasibility 4 or 5 and horizon "now": legibility layers over an existing simulation, content-elastic events with validators, salience-gated agents on a local model, and offline balancing. Each can ship as a feature of a conventional design.
  • An engine, middleware, or tools company has the infrastructure opportunities: event-sourced runtimes with model-call logging, constrained interfaces from language to game actions, headless simulation for agent testing, and calibrated surrogate libraries for weather and materials.
  • A research group has the open problems: symbolic-to-neural rendering with semantic fidelity guarantees, learned material surrogates that conserve mass and energy, automated discovery of mechanics, and evaluation of explanation quality in games.
  • Organizations outside games can use simulation games as instruments: agent benchmarks, planning sandboxes, and calibrated serious simulations, where the genre's legibility layer is as valuable as its models.

10. Risks and open problems

The opportunities in §9 inherit the risks of their techniques. Each technique records its primary risks from a closed vocabulary:

Risktechniques
Controllability34
Compute cost29
Evaluation difficulty24
Consistency / hallucination20
Latency13
Determinism11
IP / provenance9
Legibility9
Player trust / reception9
Content safety7
Labor displacement7

Consistency. Language and world models contradict state, forget, and drift. In a simulation game a contradiction is worse than a gap, because players use the simulation's outputs to build mental models. Constrained decoding, typed write-back, and grounding every generated claim in logged state are necessary; none is sufficient for open-ended generation.

Determinism. Runtime generation breaks replays, lockstep multiplayer, and bug reproduction unless outputs are recorded and replayed as events. Games that already depend on determinism (competitive leaderboards, large multiplayer factories) should treat model outputs as inputs from an external system, logged at the boundary.

Cost. Per-player-hour inference conflicts with one-time purchases and with how long simulation players play. Local models, salience gating, and caching bound cost; frame-generating world models remain far from affordable at the session lengths simulation games require (§7.2).

Legibility of learned systems. A learned policy or generated rule can be as opaque as the simulation it replaced. Every learned component that affects state needs an explanation path, or it moves a mechanic down the legibility scale in §5.6.

Evaluation. Open-ended outputs are hard to QA. Automated playtesting checks validity and balance, not quality; human evaluation does not scale to generated variety. Simulation games need evaluation methods for generated content analogous to the verification queue in this dataset: sampled, scored against anchors, and logged.

Player trust and labor. Reception of generative features has been mixed, and developers' view of generative AI's effect on the industry has turned more negative while reported use held steady (§7.2). Disclosure rules on the largest PC store already distinguish pre-generated from live-generated content [4]. Opportunities that make games more legible or let players author more (explanation, modding by description, intent-level orders) are less exposed to this risk than those that replace authored work.

Safety and provenance. Live generation in social simulations needs content guardrails, especially where players can steer characters with language. Asset generation carries training-data and likeness questions. These risks are recorded per technique so they can be filtered and tracked.

Open research problems recorded on mechanic and technique pages include: grounding generated explanations in simulation logs with measurable faithfulness; conservation guarantees for learned physics; semantic fidelity for neural rendering of symbolic state; inferring needs and preferences from behavior instead of declaring them; and fair, inspectable AI participants in player economies.

11. Predictions and research agenda

Every opportunity carries a falsifiable prediction with a resolve-by date and criteria a stranger could check. The first resolves on 2027-12-31. Because predictions are data, resolving one is a pull request: set the opportunity's status, cite the evidence, and the report and wiki update.

2028-06-30Learned build assist for citiesA city builder will ship a machine-learned layout generator that turns player strokes into detailed streets or districts.
2028-06-30Mechanic modding by descriptionThe developer of a moddable simulation game will ship or officially endorse a tool that builds working mods from natural-language descriptions.
2028-06-30Quality-diversity scenario librariesA simulation or puzzle-sim game will ship a scenario library generated by quality-diversity search.
2028-06-30Specification programming gamesA programming game will make specifying or testing AI-written code its core loop.
2028-12-31Calibrated serious simulationsA playable serious-game or educational simulation will publish posterior-calibrated parameters with fit metrics as part of its release.
2028-12-31Event-sourced simulation runtimeAn engine, middleware vendor, or open-source project will ship an event-log replay and determinism layer designed for games with generative AI components.
2028-12-31Explained delegation to AI managersA grand strategy or management game will ship AI managers that learn delegation policy from the individual player's own past decisions.
2028-12-31Generated dream and replay viewsA game will use a generative video or world model to show character memories or in-world histories drawn from the simulation's own event log.
2028-12-31Generated recipe graphsA factory or crafting game or overhaul mod will credit algorithmic or model-based generation for its recipe graph or tech tree.
2028-12-31Human-calibrated customersA management or tycoon game will state that its customer or citizen preferences come from a model of human behavior learned from data.
2028-12-31Learned regional weatherA farming, flight, or city sim will ship weather generated by a learned emulator rather than scripted states or live forecast feeds.
2028-12-31Natural-language legislationA political or city-building game will let players enact free-text laws that change simulation parameters.
2028-12-31Placement that tells storiesA city builder will advertise placement-triggered narrative events tied to named inhabitants as a core feature.
2028-12-31Salience-gated language agentsAt least three colony or life sims with over 1,000 Steam user reviews will call a language model for agents only on salient events rather than per decision.
2028-12-31Teachable sim companionAn automation or sandbox game will ship an in-game companion that learns reusable skills from player demonstration or instruction.
2029-06-30AI liquidity in player marketsA persistent online game will add AI traders to its player-driven market, with their behavior fitted to observed player trading.
2029-06-30Agent ambassadors between player worldsA game will let each player's AI representative trade or negotiate with other players' worlds while those players are offline.
2029-06-30Learned motion for simulated crowdsA management or colony sim will ship learned physics-based motion for its simulated population.
2029-06-30Negotiating faction AIA grand strategy or 4X game will ship AI opponents that negotiate in free-text or generated-language diplomacy backed by a planner.
2029-06-30Research by named scientistsA strategy or management game will ship research performed by a simulated population of named researchers whose relationships affect outcomes.
2029-06-30Trainable creatures revivalA virtual-pet or god game will ship a creature controlled by a learned neural or reinforcement-learning policy that player feedback updates during play.
2029-12-31Factories with a living workforceA factory or automation game in which workers age, train, and are replaced by a simulated next generation will reach 1,000 Steam user reviews.
2029-12-31Language-agent society terrariumA game whose core loop is observing and nudging a society of at least 50 language-model agents will reach 1,000 Steam user reviews.
2029-12-31Learned material surrogates at world scaleA game will use a learned surrogate model to simulate fluid, gas, or destruction at runtime.
2029-12-31Mean-field crowds and trafficA city builder will document a mean-field or continuum crowd model as its primary traffic or population simulation.
2029-12-31Open-ended evolution sandboxA game built on a continuous artificial-life substrate (Lenia family or neural cellular automata) will reach 1,000 Steam user reviews.
2029-12-31Participatory planning sandboxesA city government will use a game-style calibrated simulation with simulated resident feedback in a formal planning consultation.
2029-12-31Symbolic simulation, neural renderingA game will render its primary view with a generative model conditioned on an explicit symbolic game state.
2030-12-31Automated mechanic discoveryA commercial game will credit one of its shipped mechanics to an automated rule-discovery system.

Each prediction has resolution criteria on its wiki page. A prediction that fails is evidence against the opportunity thesis, not only against its timing.

11.1 Agenda

  1. Instrument a simulation for explanation. Build the event log with cause links that why-queries, branch previews, and chronicles all need, and measure explanation faithfulness against human audit.
  2. Measure legibility in players, not only in rubrics. The legibility and emergence scores here are judgments by a single model rater; a shared protocol for measuring how quickly players form correct causal models would let designers compare mechanics empirically.
  3. Connect techniques to the economic core. Production, logistics, and economy mechanics are the most used and the least targeted by current techniques (§8.2). Balance search, recipe generation, and bottleneck explanation are tractable first steps.
  4. Separate authoritative and generated layers. Develop and benchmark architectures where learned models render, narrate, or propose, and symbolic state decides.
  5. Extend the dataset. Add mobile and non-English simulation traditions, score mechanics with a second rater, resolve the verification queue, and record design tensions with evidence from postmortems.

11.2 How to extend this report

The report is generated. To add a game, mechanic, technique, or opportunity, follow AGENTS.md; tables, counts, figures, rankings, and this section's prediction list update on the next build. To change an argument, edit the prose in report/src/; every dataset number in it is a token, so the text cannot fall out of date with the data.

Appendix C. Using and extending this dataset

  • Cite a specific version by the dataset_sha256 in dist/manifest.json (also printed on this report's title page).
  • Query with the CSVs in dist/tables/, the graph files in dist/graph/ (JSON Lines, Cytoscape, GraphML), or make sqlite for SQL.
  • Browse the wiki at dist/wiki/index.md or the explorer at site/index.html.
  • Contribute by following AGENTS.md: open a run, search before creating, fill entities against the schema, run make check. The fastest useful contribution is sourcing an entity from dist/analysis/verification-queue.csv.
  • Dispute a fact by setting status: contested with a claim that cites the opposing source; disputes are data, not edits.
